title: 'Main Bhi Cockroach': India's NEET Protests Echo Across New York, London and European Cities
excerpt: Indian diaspora communities stage solidarity rallies in at least six countries as the student-led movement against exam paper leaks goes global.
body:
• Indian diaspora communities in New York, London, and European cities have staged solidarity protests echoing the 'Main bhi cockroach' (I am also a cockroach) slogan
  • The movement was founded by Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate, whose satirical Cockroach Janta Party amassed 22 million Instagram followers
  • NRIs with children studying in India or planning to return are particularly invested in the outcome of the education reform demands
  • The protests mark a rare instance of a domestic Indian social movement generating sustained diaspora mobilization across multiple continents

India's explosive student-led protests over the NEET exam paper leak have breached national borders, with Indian diaspora communities staging solidarity rallies in New York, London, and cities across Europe — chanting the movement's signature slogan, "Main bhi cockroach."

A Movement Born at Boston University

The irony is hard to miss: the protest movement shaking Modi's government was conceived by a man studying in America. Abhijeet Dipke, who completed his master's in public relations at Boston University's College of Communication, launched what he called the Cockroach Janta Party after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant referred to unemployed youth as "cockroaches."

"I made a tweet on Twitter: what if all cockroaches come together?" Dipke told the Hindu newspaper. The response was instant — 50,000 sign-ups in 24 hours, a million within five days, and 22 million Instagram followers within weeks. The pace attracted global media from the New York Times to CNN and the BBC.

"This proves that a political movement born out of satire has captured the mood of the nation and especially of the youth," Dipke said.

From Delhi Streets to Global Cities

As tens of thousands clashed with police in Delhi this week, diaspora Indians organized their own demonstrations. In New York, protesters gathered outside the Indian consulate. In London, groups rallied near India House. Similar events were reported in Toronto, Berlin, and several other European cities.

Protesters abroad carried signs reading "I am a cockroach" in English and Hindi, mirroring the movement's central act of reclaiming an insult as a badge of identity. Many shared live-streamed footage from Delhi on social media, amplifying the movement's reach.

Why NRIs Care

The NEET crisis cuts close to home for diaspora families. Many NRIs have relatives — children, nieces, nephews — preparing for India's notoriously competitive entrance exams. The leak of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test, which is the sole gateway to undergraduate medical courses, affected roughly 2 million students and was linked to about a dozen suicides.

For NRI parents considering sending children to study medicine in India, or those whose families invested years and significant money in NEET preparation, the systemic failure represents more than a policy issue — it's a betrayal of the meritocratic promise that Indian education is supposed to offer.

"What if all cockroaches come together?"

— Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, in the tweet that launched the movement

Digital Amplification

The movement's global reach owes much to its digital DNA. Unlike traditional Indian protests organized through political parties, the CJP spread through Instagram memes, X threads, and WhatsApp groups — the same channels diaspora communities use to stay connected with home.

The original X page for the party was taken down in India, and pro-government media figures like Arnab Goswami have attempted to discredit the movement, calling it "a sign of a multi-pronged attack against India." But the movement's decentralized, social-media-first structure has made it difficult to contain.

What Comes Next

As Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan pledged this week to discuss NEET reforms in Parliament, diaspora organizers say they will maintain pressure until concrete steps are taken. The protests mark a rare instance where a domestic Indian social movement has generated sustained, multi-city mobilization among overseas Indian communities — a sign that the 18-million-strong Indian diaspora increasingly views itself as a stakeholder in India's governance, not merely its economy.
